title: Lior and the Harbor
premise: Rosalind Okafor, a celebrated cellist whose hands froze mid-concert in front of two thousand people, retreats to the fading harbor town of Greywater Bay to teach and to hide. There she discovers that her late grandmother's house came with an inheritance stranger than furniture: ten years of letters from a secret admirer she never answered, written by Theo Marsh, the lighthouse keeper's son who has just moved in next door. As Rosalind relearns her instrument through Theo's patient presence, she uncovers that his family's shipping fortune was built on debts her grandmother quietly forgave—and that the letters stopped only because Theo was losing his sight. When a prestigious orchestra offers Rosalind a comeback on the same night Theo faces surgery that may not restore his vision, she must choose between the stage that once betrayed her and the man who taught her that memory, like music, is something you play forward. She performs at the harbor itself, dedicating the concert to him, and chooses love over legacy—only to learn he chose her first, having declined the operation to keep one last season of seeing her clearly.
about_author: August Eastwick is the pen name of a former orchestral librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's masterpieces before writing her own. She lives on a cold coast with a dog named Fermata and writes about people who mistake silence for safety.

chapters.title: The Silence After
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Eight months after her catastrophic final performance, she unpacks in her inherited grandmother's house in Greywater Bay, refusing to open the cello case. The chapter establishes her rule: the heart is a muscle; you train it not to feel. Emotional beat: brittle control masking grief.

chapters.title: Letters in the Attic
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Sorting her grandmother's belongings, she finds a locked tin containing ten years of unsigned letters addressed to her, postmarked from this very town—letters forwarded by her grandmother and never delivered. The last one is dated three years ago. Beat: vertigo; someone knew her intimately while she performed for strangers.

chapters.title: The New Neighbor
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo Marsh moves into the cottage next door with crates of books and a white cane he doesn't yet need. He recognizes Rosalind immediately but says nothing, honoring a promise made to her grandmother. Beat: tenderness tangled with guilt as he watches her carry the unopened cello case inside.

chapters.title: Salt and Scales
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Forced into town for groceries, Rosalind hears someone practicing a simple folk melody on a battered piano at the community hall. Her hands ache to answer it. She flees home and, alone, opens the case for the first time—playing four bars before stopping. Beat: the first crack in her armor.

chapters.title: A Decade of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Dual POV. A neighbor's garden party throws them together; Theo quotes a line from the letters verbatim without realizing, and Rosalind goes cold. Suspicion blooms: is the letter-writer mocking her? Beat: attraction curdling into wariness, each hiding what they know.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Kept
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Reading deeper into the letters, she learns the writer watched her grandmother decline, ran her errands, and wrote about 'the girl on the stage' with devastating specificity. She also finds a ledger: her grandmother forgave enormous debts owed by the Marsh shipping firm. Beat: the inheritance is more complicated than money—it's obligation.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Son
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Flashback woven through present: how Theo began writing after hearing fourteen-year-old Rosalind play at a summer festival, and how his father's failing business was saved by old Mrs. Okafor's quiet mercy—a debt Theo repaid by watching over her granddaughter from afar. Beat: shame at loving through paper instead of presence.

chapters.title: Duet, Unrehearsed
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Storm knocks out power; Rosalind, candlelit and reckless, plays the folk melody from the hall. Theo appears at her door with his violin. They play together in the dark where she cannot see his face and he cannot fully see hers. Beat: intimacy achieved precisely because sight is absent.

chapters.title: Terms of Inheritance
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The town solicitor reveals the will's condition: the house and a trust are hers outright—but a scholarship fund in her name requires her to perform publicly within the year, or it dissolves. Her comeback is now contractual. Beat: rage at being managed even from the grave.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Waterline
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Rosalind accuses Theo of being the letter-writer and of colluding with her grandmother. He admits everything except why the letters stopped. She walks out. Beat: the relationship breaks on the very truth that created it.

chapters.title: The Empty Page
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Alone, Theo rereads his unsent final letter—the one explaining his diagnosis: retinal degeneration, a narrowing window of sight. His grandmother's promise to Mrs. Okafor bound him to silence until Rosalind was ready. Beat: grief for the years fear cost him.

chapters.title: Winter Harbor
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Weeks of silence. Rosalind teaches a stubborn twelve-year-old student and realizes she's been teaching avoidance, not music. Watching Theo navigate the icy dock alone, nearly falling, she understands his pride and her own are the same disease. Beat: empathy replacing anger.

chapters.title: Reading by Touch
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo begins learning braille and memorizing the routes of the town before winter deepens. Rosalind starts leaving food on his porch without notes—an apology in the language of care they both understand. Beat: reconciliation begun wordlessly.

chapters.title: The Comeback Offer
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The Meridian Symphony calls: a principal cellist position, the career she thought dead, audition in six weeks in the city. Everyone tells her it's salvation. But the audition date conflicts with the scholarship deadline performance she'd planned for the harbor. Beat: the old dream returns wearing new chains.

chapters.title: Confessions in C Minor
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Rosalind finally reads the last letter aloud to Theo, demanding the truth. He tells her about his eyes, the surgery scheduled in spring with uncertain odds, and why he refused to be pitied or managed. She tells him about the night her hands failed and what it cost. Beat: total honesty; love becomes possible.

chapters.title: What Power Owes
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Digging into the ledger, Rosalind discovers her grandmother's forgiveness wasn't pure charity—the Okafor fortune had ruined the Marshes first, a generation back. Inheritance runs both directions: wealth and wound. Beat: Rosalind reframes her legacy as debt to be paid, not prize to keep.

chapters.title: Two Stages
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo secretly contacts the Meridian Symphony to withdraw on Rosalind's behalf, believing she'll sacrifice the harbor concert—and the trust—for him. Rosalind discovers the call. Furious, she accuses him of doing exactly what her grandmother did: deciding for her. Beat: the central theme detonates—love that manages is corruption.

chapters.title: The Broken Bow
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. In despair, Rosalind snaps her bow during practice and, in the wreckage, finally plays the piece she abandoned onstage—the full concerto, alone, weeping, complete. She realizes the failure wasn't her hands; it was performing for approval instead of meaning. Beat: the artistic breakthrough that makes choice possible.

chapters.title: Surgery Eve
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Theo checks into the hospital, having reversed his decision—he'll take the odds, because refusing treatment was another form of hiding. Rosalind comes to his room. No declarations; she simply plays for him, softly, on a borrowed instrument, and promises nothing except tomorrow. Beat: quiet vow beneath uncertainty.

chapters.title: Concert at the Harbor
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The scholarship deadline arrives. Rosalind stages the required performance on the frozen harbor itself, the whole town gathered, playing the concerto she once fled—dedicated to 'the person behind a decade of letters.' Bandages still on his eyes, Theo listens from the front row. Beat: triumph redefined as presence, not perfection.

chapters.title: What the Light Returns
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The bandages come off. Sight returns partially—blurred edges, but enough. Theo walks to the harbor house where Rosalind has declined the symphony's relocation, choosing instead a visiting-artist residency that lets her teach here and tour on her own terms. Beat: both have chosen visibility over safety.

chapters.title: Lior and the Harbor
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Spring. Rosalind writes the first letter of a new correspondence and hand-delivers it next door; Theo answers in person. The epilogue braids their voices: the heart is a muscle, yes—but its training is courage, practiced daily. Final image: two instruments playing the folk melody as the tide turns. Beat: earned, unhurried peace.
